blocks.prompt: The Nest That Kept Growing
blocks.text: An eagle builds the biggest tree nest of any bird. It picks the tallest tree it can find. It carries sticks up in its feet, one at a time. It lays the sticks in a big circle and packs soft grass in the middle. The next year the eagle comes back to the same nest. It adds more sticks. It does this every year, and the nest gets bigger and bigger. Some eagle nests get so heavy that the branch under them breaks. Baby eagles are called eaglets. They sit in the nest and wait. When a parent lands with a fish, they all start to squeak.

blocks.prompt: The Eye in the Sky
blocks.text: An eagle can spot a fish from a mile away. You could stand on the shore and see nothing but water. The eagle, circling high above you, sees the fish turn. The secret is in the back of the eye. Your eye has one small patch where your sharpest seeing happens. An eagle has two of them in each eye, and each patch is packed with far more light-catching cells than yours. That is why an eagle can hold the whole lake in view and still pick out one moving shape in it. Eagles have another trick. They have a third eyelid, a thin clear one that sweeps sideways across the eye. It wipes the eye clean and shields it in a dive, and the eagle can still see through it. Once the eagle picks its fish, it drops. It swings its feet forward at the last second and hits the water. An eagle's toes are covered underneath in little rough bumps that bite into slippery scales. Then it beats its way back into the air, dripping, with dinner.

two

(inference: fish are slippery and would slide out of a smooth foot)

4.title: The Eagle That Isn't What You Think
4.subtitle: A reading and science sheet for ages 9 to 10

meta.templateLabel: The Eagle That Isn't What You Think

blocks.prompt: Read the passage, then work through each part.

notes: The movie eagle scream is really a red-tailed hawk
A real bald eagle makes a thin squeaky whistle

blocks.prompt: The Sound You Think You Know
blocks.text: You have heard an eagle scream. In every movie where a lone bird circles over a canyon, the same long, rasping cry comes down out of the sky. It sounds like power itself. It is not an eagle. It is a red-tailed hawk. A real bald eagle sounds nothing like that. It makes a thin, chattering whistle, a string of high squeaks that would not frighten anybody. Sound engineers decided long ago that the real call did not match the bird's face, so they dubbed the hawk over the top of it. Almost everyone alive has now heard a hawk and believed it was an eagle. The rest of the eagle's reputation is complicated too. Bald eagles are superb hunters, but they are also thieves. An eagle will watch an osprey work for its fish, then chase it until the smaller bird drops the catch, and take it out of the air. Eagles eat animals that are already dead. They stand on frozen lakes and wait. They cannot carry off much, either. A bald eagle weighs somewhere around ten pounds, and it cannot lift much more than a few pounds into the air. The old stories about eagles snatching lambs and babies are stories. What an eagle actually does, when it grabs a fish too heavy to fly with, is refuse to let go. It spreads its wings out on the surface and rows itself to shore, hauling its dinner behind it like a slow, furious swimmer. None of this makes the eagle less impressive. It only makes it real. The bird on the flag is not the bird on the lake.

5.title: The Eagle That Isn't What You Think
5.subtitle: A reading and science sheet for ages 11 to 12
5.intro: Read the passage, then answer in full sentences. Use evidence from the text where the question asks for it.

meta.templateLabel: The Eagle That Isn't What You Think

blocks.prompt: Read the passage, then work through each part.

notes: Haliaeetus leucocephalus
1963: only 417 nesting pairs left in the lower 48 states
DDT made their eggshells too thin to sit on
The US banned DDT in 1972
Taken off the endangered species list in 2007
About 71,400 nesting pairs counted in 2021

blocks.prompt: Four Hundred and Seventeen
blocks.text: In 1963, biologists went looking for bald eagles across the lower forty-eight states and found 417 nesting pairs. Four hundred and seventeen. For a bird spread across a continent, that is a rounding error away from gone. The eagles were not being shot in numbers that could explain it, and they were not starving. They were laying eggs that broke. A parent would settle onto the clutch to keep it warm, as eagles have done for millions of years, and the shells would collapse under her own weight. The cause was a pesticide called DDT, sprayed across American farmland after the Second World War to kill insects. DDT does not stay where it is sprayed. It washed into rivers, where tiny organisms absorbed it, and small fish ate those organisms, and larger fish ate those small fish. At every step the chemical concentrated instead of clearing. Biologists call this biomagnification. The animal at the top of the chain inherits everything the chain has collected, and on an American lake, the animal at the top of the chain is a bald eagle. Inside the eagle, DDT interfered with the process that lays calcium into an eggshell. The shells came out thin. The birds were poisoned not in their bodies but in their next generation, which is a quieter and much more effective way to erase a species. The United States banned DDT in 1972. What happened next is the part worth remembering. The eagles were not clever, or resilient, or lucky. Nothing about the bird changed. The poison simply stopped arriving, laws made it a crime to kill them, and the shells thickened back up. Slowly, then quickly, the eagles returned. By 2007 the bald eagle came off the endangered species list. A recent federal survey estimated more than seventy thousand nesting pairs in the same states where four hundred and seventeen had been found. There is a lesson in there that is easy to miss, because it is unglamorous. The eagles did not come back because people loved them. Plenty of species have been loved into extinction. They came back because a specific chemical was identified, argued about, and outlawed, and then people waited about forty years. Rescue, when it works, tends to look like paperwork.

6.title: The Eagle That Isn't What You Think
6.subtitle: A reading and history sheet for age 13
6.intro: Read the passage closely, then answer in full sentences. Cite the text directly where a question asks for evidence.

meta.templateLabel: The Eagle That Isn't What You Think

blocks.prompt: Read the passage, then work through each part.

notes: Haliaeetus leucocephalus
On the Great Seal since June 20, 1782
Officially named the national bird in December 2024
Franklin called it a bird of bad moral character
Kleptoparasite: it robs ospreys of their catch
Its feathers weigh more than twice its skeleton

blocks.prompt: The Bird on the Money
blocks.text: On June 20, 1782, the Continental Congress adopted a national seal with a bald eagle at the center of it, wings spread, an olive branch clutched in one foot and a bundle of thirteen arrows in the other. The bird has been on American coins, passports, podiums, and military badges ever since. Almost every citizen would have told you, at any point in the last two centuries, that the bald eagle was the national bird of the United States. It was not. Not officially. The seal made it the emblem on a piece of government stationery, and everything after that was habit. Congress did not actually name the bald eagle the national bird until December 2024, which means that for two hundred and forty-two years the most recognizable national symbol in the world held its position on nothing but assumption. Benjamin Franklin, for one, was not impressed. In a private letter to his daughter in 1784, he complained that the eagle on the badge of a new society of army officers was 'a Bird of bad moral Character' who 'does not get his Living honestly,' because it sits in trees and robs hardworking fishing hawks of the fish they catch. He was not proposing the turkey as a replacement, whatever you have been told, though he did call the turkey 'a much more respectable Bird.' He was making a joke in a letter. It survived because it landed on something true. Franklin's accusation is, biologically, accurate. Bald eagles are kleptoparasites: they take food other animals have caught. An eagle will harass an osprey in midair until it releases its fish, then catch the fish before it hits the water. Bald eagles also scavenge carrion and gather at dumps and fish-processing plants, which is not the behavior anyone had in mind for the emblem of a republic. The gap between the symbol and the animal widens from there. The scream you associate with an eagle, the one that plays over every wide shot of a mountain, belongs to a red-tailed hawk. Sound engineers substituted it decades ago because the bald eagle's actual voice, a thin chittering whistle, struck them as insufficiently majestic. The country's symbol has been redubbed for the country's benefit. And then there is the number 417. In 1963, that was the count of bald eagle nesting pairs left in the lower forty-eight states, brought there by DDT thinning their eggshells until the parents crushed their own eggs. The nation that had put this bird on its currency very nearly finished it off with agricultural runoff. The eagle recovered only after 1972, when DDT was banned, and it was formally taken off the endangered species list in 2007. So consider what the symbol is actually made of. A magnificent hunter that steals. A voice we replaced. A national bird that was not legally a national bird until 2024. A species we almost erased while stamping it onto our money. You can read that as a case against the eagle. You can also read it the other way. A symbol that only reflected our best qualities would be a portrait, not a mirror. The bald eagle is opportunistic, occasionally undignified, nearly lost, and back, and it is the one bird in America whose story is honest enough to hold all of that at once.
